**Vasilopita** (Greek: Βασιλόπιτα, _Vasilópita_, lit. '(St.) Basil-pie' or 'Vassilis pie', see below) is a [New Year's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Day "New Year's Day") bread, cake or pie in Greece and throughout Southeastern Europe which contains a hidden coin or trinket which gives good luck to the receiver, like the Western European king cake. It is associated with [Saint Basil's day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Basil's_day "Saint Basil's day"), 1 January, in most of Greece, but in some regions, the traditions surrounding a cake or pita with a hidden coin are attached to Epiphany or to Christmas. It is made of a variety of dough, depending on regional and family tradition, including tsoureki. In some families, instead of dough, it is made from a custard base called galatopita (literally milk-pita). In the Thessaly region a pork filled phyllo pie is made with a hidden coin. The pie is also known as _Chronópita_ (Χρονόπιτα < χρόνος: _chrónos ⇨ time/year_ + πίτα: _píta ⇨ pie_), meaning "New Year's pie".
In other areas of the Balkans, the tradition of cake with a hidden coin during winter holidays exists, but is not associated with Saint Basil at all. The practice is documented among Ukrainians (a pirog is cut); Romanians; Serbs ("česnica", eaten on Christmas); Albanians ("pite" or “kulaç”, eaten by both Christians and Muslims); Bulgarians (_pogacha_, _Novogodishna banitsa_ (for New Year's), _Svety Vasileva pogacha_); etc.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-hasluck-1)

On New Year's Day families cut the vasilopita to bless the house and bring good luck for the new year. This is usually done at the midnight of New Year's Eve. A coin is hidden in the bread by slipping it into the dough before baking. At midnight the sign of the cross is etched with a knife across the cake. A piece of cake is sliced for each member of the family and any visitors present at the time, by order of age from eldest to youngest. Slices are also cut for various symbolic people or groups, depending on local and family tradition. They may include the Lord, St. Basil and other saints, the poor, the household, or the Kallikantzaroi. In older times, the coin often was a valuable one, such as a gold sovereign. Nowadays there is often a prearranged gift, money, or otherwise, to be given to the coin recipient._[citation needed_]
Many private or public institutions, such as societies, clubs, workplaces, companies, etc., cut their vasilopita at a convenient time between New Year's Day and the beginning of the Great Fast, in celebrations that range from impromptu potluck gatherings to formal receptions or balls._[citation needed_]
Saint Basil's Feast Day is observed on 1 January, the beginning of the New Year and the Epiphany season known as the _Vasilopita Observance_._[citation needed_]
Margaret Hasluck (1927) disputes the historicity of the Greek folk tradition of celebrating the feast day of St. Basil with _vasilopita_. She says the popular belief is based on a "false etymology". Hasluck arrives at this conclusion by comparing the traditions of Greek-speaking communities with the western European celebrations of the Twelfth Night and Epiphany. Hasluck notes that no document mentions the _basilopita_, although Gregory of Nyssa confirms the festival of Basil was one of the feast days that succeeded Christmas in his time:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-hasluck-1)
> After [Christmas] the spiritual dance was opened by apostles and prophets...These are Stephen, Peter, James, John, and Paul. Then after them, in his due order, the pastor and teacher initiates our present gathering. Who is this? ... I mean Basil, the man of noble life and speech.

Hasluck speculates that the etymology connecting the tradition to Basil's feast day is erroneous. She proposes that the translation "cake of the king" (from _basileus_) is as accurate as the translation "cake of basil", a claim that she says is supported by the similarity in customs of the hidden coin and the hidden bean. She refers to _Larousse Gastronomique'_ s description of the _fève_ custom referring to the _gateau des rois_ (popularly known as king cake in English) associated in present times with the Christian holiday of Epiphany celebrated on the "Twelfth Night" after Christmas. She disputes the Christian origin of the holiday: "We may safely dismiss the theory of their Christian origin and recognize, with many good authorities, in the Twelve Days the relics of a purely pagan festival." According to Hasluck, the pagan holiday of the Twelve Days is the same as the Roman Saturnalia: "One feature of the Saturnalia was that men drew for a king with a bean, and held high revelry under his leadership for the duration of the festivities", which she says is the same as the Greek festival Kronia: "Consequently, with some confidence we identify the Basil of the _basilopita_ with the _basileus_, the "king" of Saaturnalia".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-hasluck-1)

Nonetheless, in popular tradition, vasilopita is associated with a legend of Basil of Caesarea. According to one story, Basil called on the Roman citizens of Caesarea to raise a ransom payment to stop the siege of the city. Each member of the city gave whatever they had in gold and jewelry. When the ransom was raised, the enemy was so embarrassed by the act of collective giving that he called off the siege without collecting payment. Basil was then tasked with returning the unpaid ransom, but had no way to know which items belonged to which family so he baked all of the jewellery into loaves of bread and distributed the loaves to the city, and by a miracle each citizen received their exact share. In some tellings, the sieging tribal chief is replaced with an evil emperor levying a tax or simply with Basil attempting to give charity to the poor without embarrassing them.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-vasilopita.com-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-antiochian-3)_[better source needed_]
The name "βασιλόπιτα" comes from βασιλεύς 'king' + πίτα 'cake', but was reinterpreted as "Basil's (Βασίλειος) cake".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-hasluck-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-CFVM-5) In Cyprus it is also known as vasilopoulla ("βασιλοπούλλα").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-CFVM-5)

## The meaning of the vasilopita
Ever wonder why, in most Greek families, names seem to be on repeat? At any family function you are likely to find 4 Marias, 3 Costas and about 7 Georges. That’s because Greek parents have traditionally always named their children after their own parents. So, two siblings who each have daughters, may very well name their girls after their common mother, for example. Many Greek names are also names of Saints, making the Nameday (the day on which we commemorate the life of a given Saint) a much bigger deal amongst many Greeks than birthdays could ever be. Each of us is named after one of our grandmothers, and one of our Greek names (Vasiliki) is also associated with Saint Basil the Great, who is commemorated on January 1st, the day of his death.
St. Basil the Great was the Greek bishop of Caesarea Mazaca in Coppadocia, in Asia Minor (what is today, Turkey). In addition to his theological works, he was also a great support for the underprivileged and poor. In his memory, on St. Basil’s Day, homes of Orthodox Christians serve vasilopita (translated to mean _St. Basil’s bread_) to honour him. Although there are many versions and types of vasilopita, they all have one thing in common; there is a single coin baked into each one. This coin is a symbol and reminder of St. Basil’s intervention against the emperor of Caesarea, and God’s miracle. One year, the emperor of Caesarea had levied a heavy tax on the people, during a year of great famine and hardship. Upon hearing the news, St. Basil asked the emperor to repent, and he did. The emperor ordered that all gold coins, money and jewels that the people had used to pay this tax, be returned to them. Bishop Basil was assigned the daunting and overwhelming task of doing so. Unsure of how to return the goods to their rightful owners, prayer led St. Basil to bake a large pita, into which he inserted all the valuables. He then called the townspeople to each take a piece. Miraculously, each person received a piece of vasilopita that contained the exact items which were to be returned to them.

## How to serve vasilopita
In my family, vasilopita is always served after lunch on the Feast Day of St. Basil, which is coincidentally also New Year’s Day (January 1st) for many. Our father is typically the person who cuts and serves the pieces, and this is done in a particular order. The first piece is cut and saved for Christ, the second for St. Basil, and the third for the less fortunate. Then, a piece of vasilopita is cut for all members of the family, and any friends who may be present. The vasilopita is always offered first to the oldest person present, up until the youngest. The person whose piece contains the coin is expected to have good luck and blessings for the upcoming year.

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Mix your batter carefully
Unlike cooking, where you can take some liberties, and perhaps even some shortcuts, baking really is a science. There are many pitfalls you can encounter when baking, which is why it is important to find reliable recipes (like the ones here at Mia Kouppa) and follow them carefully.
One of the important things to keep in mind when you are making vasilopita is how the batter comes together. Sometimes you will bake a cake and end up with streaks, or areas of dense, sodden cake. These give the impression that the cake is under-baked – even though it’s completely baked. In order to prevent this from happening, you must beat together the sugar, butter and eggs, slowly; your mixer should not go any higher than medium speed.
Then, when you add the dry ingredients, the mixing speed has to be slower still. By keeping the mixer speed at medium and lower you avoid developing the flour’s gluten too much; which will help avoid your cake sinking in the middle once you take it out of the oven. It is this sinking which creates dense, moist, gluey streaks in your cake. .

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### How to prepare your cake pan
Although you will grease your cake pan with some vegetable oil, is it still a very good idea to line the bottom of the pan with parchment paper. The easiest way to get just the right size of parchment paper for the bottom of your round pan is to place your baking pan on a sheet of parchment paper and to trace its outline with a pencil. Then, use a scissor to cut out the perfect circle. Ta da!

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Inserting the coin into your cake batter
Before inserting the coin into your cake batter, it is a very good idea to wash it and to then wrap it with either food grade plastic wrap or aluminum foil. You can even use parchment paper, although that can be a little more cumbersome to wrap the coin in. Traditionally, before inserting the coin into the cake you would use it to make the sign of the cross over the pan. The easiest way to get your coin into the batter is to use a knife to make a small cut into the batter and slip the coin right in. Spread the batter evenly so that it is not obvious where the coin is.

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### How to display the year on your vasilopita
There are many ways to bake a vasilopita. Some versions are very bread-like, and similar to the Easter tsoureki. Other versions, like this recipe, are more cake-like. Both are delicious, but different. Besides the obvious flavour and texture differences, another difference between the two is that with the bread type of vasilopita you can usually use a bit of the dough to roll out the numbers of the year, which is then laid on top of the bread before baking. You can’t really do that with this recipe. If you would like to have the year showcased on your vasilopita however, you can either decorate it with sliced almonds, or use a stencil with the year cut out of it, on top of the cake before you sprinkle it with icing sugar. My parents would sometimes do this, but not usually. They always reminded us that this was not a New Year’s cake, but a cake to commemorate the Feast Day of St. Basil.

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Serve and eat your vasilopita with care
Eating cake or bread with a coin hidden in it could definitely be a choking hazard, so please…if you are serving vasilopita to the very young or the very elderly, be careful. I remember that when me and my siblings were little, our parents would often tear our pieces apart before allowing us to eat them, being sure that if there was a coin in our piece, it would be found before it ended up in our mouths. Now that I think of it…I can’t remember a year when one of the children didn’t actually get the coin. Coincidence? Maybe…or perhaps clever serving by our dad. It was always such a thrill to find the coin!

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Best when served the day after it is made
This cake keeps really well and is even more delicious if made the day before. This is also a great option because it means that your cake will have ample time to cool fully before you sprinkle it with icing sugar.

## Recipe variations
### Make vasilopita cupcakes
If you will only be a few people gathering in New Year’s Day it is hard to divide up the vasilopita completely in order to be sure that someone gets the coin. There ends up being a lot of wasted cake if, for example, four people share the entire vasilopita.
That is why there are vasilopita cupcakes! Learn how to make this not-quite-traditional-but-absolutely-brilliant version of vasilopita. This way you ensure that the coin will be found, everyone has an appropriate amount of the vasilopita, and there is no waste! Learn how to make them by following this recipe for vasilopita cupcakes.

Stir dry ingredients and make a well in the center. After the yeast is doubled in size, add yeast, 1 more cup of warm milk, 2 tablespoons olive oil, 4 beaten eggs, and the zest of one orange. Mix together until a smooth dough forms _(add up to 1/2 cup more flour if necessary)_.
Knead the dough on floured surface for about 10 minutes _(or continue kneading in your mixer if you prefer)_.
Swirl some oil in the bottom of a large bowl. Place the kneaded dough inside and turn once, allowing the oil to coat the top of the dough. This prevents drying out/cracking when the dough rises. Allow to rise in a warm place for 1-2 hours, or until about doubled in size.

When I need to let dough rise, I usually turn on the oven light, turn on the temperature on for 1 minute, allow it to warm up slightly, and immediately turn the heat off. Then, I place the dough in the oven to rise. The residual heat as well as the heat from the oven light will keep a toasty _(but not TOO toasty)_ environment for the dough to rise.
Punch dough down and divide into two. Knead each for a few minutes and form into two balls. Butter two nine-inch round pans and place the dough balls in the middle of each. Place back in a warm area, covered with a kitchen towel, to allow to rise again for about 1 hour.
Man, did I get a lot of new year’s day cleaning done while the dough was rising!
Now comes the fun part!
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees F. Once the dough has doubled in size again, use a sharp knife or clean razor blade to carve a pattern in the top of your dough. You can do any design you want, and a lot of people will write out the numbers of the year, or a cross shape, but it’s easy to start with lines that radiate from the center _(curved or straight)_. Then, you can add other lines to connect them.

When they are done, allow them to cool for 10 minutes in the pan, then take them out of the pans and allow to cool on a rack. You may need to run a knife along the edge to separate it from the side of the pan.
At this point, you can insert a coin _(I usually use a dime since it’s small)_ through the bottom of one of the loaves, pushing it through with a toothpick or skinny knife.

Stir dry ingredients and make a well in the center. After the yeast is doubled in size, add yeast, 1 more cup of warm milk, 2 tablespoons olive oil, 4 beaten eggs, and the zest of one orange. Mix together until a smooth dough forms _(add up to 1/2 cup more flour if necessary)_.
Knead the dough on floured surface for about 10 minutes _(or continue kneading in your mixer if you prefer)_.
Swirl some oil in the bottom of a large bowl. Place the kneaded dough inside and turn once, allowing the oil to coat the top of the dough. This prevents drying out/cracking when the dough rises. Allow to rise in a warm place for 1-2 hours, or until about doubled in size.
texts.4:
When I need to let dough rise, I usually turn on the oven light, turn on the temperature on for 1 minute, allow it to warm up slightly, and immediately turn the heat off. Then, I place the dough in the oven to rise. The residual heat as well as the heat from the oven light will keep a toasty _(but not TOO toasty)_ environment for the dough to rise.
Punch dough down and divide into two. Knead each for a few minutes and form into two balls. Butter two nine-inch round pans and place the dough balls in the middle of each. Place back in a warm area, covered with a kitchen towel, to allow to rise again for about 1 hour.
Man, did I get a lot of new year’s day cleaning done while the dough was rising!
Now comes the fun part!
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees F. Once the dough has doubled in size again, use a sharp knife or clean razor blade to carve a pattern in the top of your dough. You can do any design you want, and a lot of people will write out the numbers of the year, or a cross shape, but it’s easy to start with lines that radiate from the center _(curved or straight)_. Then, you can add other lines to connect them.
![Image 4: Process collage showing brushing Vasilopita with egg wash.](blob:http://localhost/f92e3f3f2b0eef422e60d765f2c16257)
![Image 5: Process collage showing brushing Vasilopita with egg wash.](blob:http://localhost/f92e3f3f2b0eef422e60d765f2c16257)
I got a little fancy and did a vine with leaves coming out from it.
FINALLY, beat one egg and brush the top of each loaf with it to cover it. Sprinkle with sesame seeds _(some people use slices almonds instead)_, and bake for 10 minutes at 375 degrees F.
Turn the temperature down to 350 degrees F and bake for another 30 minutes, or until the loaves turn a deep chestnut brown on top.

When they are done, allow them to cool for 10 minutes in the pan, then take them out of the pans and allow to cool on a rack. You may need to run a knife along the edge to separate it from the side of the pan.
At this point, you can insert a coin _(I usually use a dime since it’s small)_ through the bottom of one of the loaves, pushing it through with a toothpick or skinny knife.
Yes, this is probably a choking hazard. Watch your little ones!
There we go! Done! Phew!

## The meaning of the vasilopita
Ever wonder why, in most Greek families, names seem to be on repeat? At any family function you are likely to find 4 Marias, 3 Costas and about 7 Georges. That’s because Greek parents have traditionally always named their children after their own parents. So, two siblings who each have daughters, may very well name their girls after their common mother, for example. Many Greek names are also names of Saints, making the Nameday (the day on which we commemorate the life of a given Saint) a much bigger deal amongst many Greeks than birthdays could ever be. Each of us is named after one of our grandmothers, and one of our Greek names (Vasiliki) is also associated with Saint Basil the Great, who is commemorated on January 1st, the day of his death.
St. Basil the Great was the Greek bishop of Caesarea Mazaca in Coppadocia, in Asia Minor (what is today, Turkey). In addition to his theological works, he was also a great support for the underprivileged and poor. In his memory, on St. Basil’s Day, homes of Orthodox Christians serve vasilopita (translated to mean _St. Basil’s bread_) to honour him. Although there are many versions and types of vasilopita, they all have one thing in common; there is a single coin baked into each one. This coin is a symbol and reminder of St. Basil’s intervention against the emperor of Caesarea, and God’s miracle. One year, the emperor of Caesarea had levied a heavy tax on the people, during a year of great famine and hardship. Upon hearing the news, St. Basil asked the emperor to repent, and he did. The emperor ordered that all gold coins, money and jewels that the people had used to pay this tax, be returned to them. Bishop Basil was assigned the daunting and overwhelming task of doing so. Unsure of how to return the goods to their rightful owners, prayer led St. Basil to bake a large pita, into which he inserted all the valuables. He then called the townspeople to each take a piece. Miraculously, each person received a piece of vasilopita that contained the exact items which were to be returned to them.

## How to serve vasilopita
In my family, vasilopita is always served after lunch on the Feast Day of St. Basil, which is coincidentally also New Year’s Day (January 1st) for many. Our father is typically the person who cuts and serves the pieces, and this is done in a particular order. The first piece is cut and saved for Christ, the second for St. Basil, and the third for the less fortunate. Then, a piece of vasilopita is cut for all members of the family, and any friends who may be present. The vasilopita is always offered first to the oldest person present, up until the youngest. The person whose piece contains the coin is expected to have good luck and blessings for the upcoming year.

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Mix your batter carefully
Unlike cooking, where you can take some liberties, and perhaps even some shortcuts, baking really is a science. There are many pitfalls you can encounter when baking, which is why it is important to find reliable recipes (like the ones here at Mia Kouppa) and follow them carefully.
One of the important things to keep in mind when you are making vasilopita is how the batter comes together. Sometimes you will bake a cake and end up with streaks, or areas of dense, sodden cake. These give the impression that the cake is under-baked – even though it’s completely baked. In order to prevent this from happening, you must beat together the sugar, butter and eggs, slowly; your mixer should not go any higher than medium speed.
Then, when you add the dry ingredients, the mixing speed has to be slower still. By keeping the mixer speed at medium and lower you avoid developing the flour’s gluten too much; which will help avoid your cake sinking in the middle once you take it out of the oven. It is this sinking which creates dense, moist, gluey streaks in your cake. .

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### How to prepare your cake pan
Although you will grease your cake pan with some vegetable oil, is it still a very good idea to line the bottom of the pan with parchment paper. The easiest way to get just the right size of parchment paper for the bottom of your round pan is to place your baking pan on a sheet of parchment paper and to trace its outline with a pencil. Then, use a scissor to cut out the perfect circle. Ta da!

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Inserting the coin into your cake batter
Before inserting the coin into your cake batter, it is a very good idea to wash it and to then wrap it with either food grade plastic wrap or aluminum foil. You can even use parchment paper, although that can be a little more cumbersome to wrap the coin in. Traditionally, before inserting the coin into the cake you would use it to make the sign of the cross over the pan. The easiest way to get your coin into the batter is to use a knife to make a small cut into the batter and slip the coin right in. Spread the batter evenly so that it is not obvious where the coin is.
texts.14:
## Baking tips and helpful hints
### How to display the year on your vasilopita
There are many ways to bake a vasilopita. Some versions are very bread-like, and similar to the Easter tsoureki. Other versions, like this recipe, are more cake-like. Both are delicious, but different. Besides the obvious flavour and texture differences, another difference between the two is that with the bread type of vasilopita you can usually use a bit of the dough to roll out the numbers of the year, which is then laid on top of the bread before baking. You can’t really do that with this recipe. If you would like to have the year showcased on your vasilopita however, you can either decorate it with sliced almonds, or use a stencil with the year cut out of it, on top of the cake before you sprinkle it with icing sugar. My parents would sometimes do this, but not usually. They always reminded us that this was not a New Year’s cake, but a cake to commemorate the Feast Day of St. Basil.
texts.15:
## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Serve and eat your vasilopita with care
Eating cake or bread with a coin hidden in it could definitely be a choking hazard, so please…if you are serving vasilopita to the very young or the very elderly, be careful. I remember that when me and my siblings were little, our parents would often tear our pieces apart before allowing us to eat them, being sure that if there was a coin in our piece, it would be found before it ended up in our mouths. Now that I think of it…I can’t remember a year when one of the children didn’t actually get the coin. Coincidence? Maybe…or perhaps clever serving by our dad. It was always such a thrill to find the coin!
texts.16:
## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Best when served the day after it is made
This cake keeps really well and is even more delicious if made the day before. This is also a great option because it means that your cake will have ample time to cool fully before you sprinkle it with icing sugar.

## Recipe variations
### Make vasilopita cupcakes
If you will only be a few people gathering in New Year’s Day it is hard to divide up the vasilopita completely in order to be sure that someone gets the coin. There ends up being a lot of wasted cake if, for example, four people share the entire vasilopita.
That is why there are vasilopita cupcakes! Learn how to make this not-quite-traditional-but-absolutely-brilliant version of vasilopita. This way you ensure that the coin will be found, everyone has an appropriate amount of the vasilopita, and there is no waste! Learn how to make them by following this recipe for vasilopita cupcakes.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Type Bread or cake  
Place of originGreece or Cyprus
*   Media: Vasilopita
**Vasilopita** (Greek: Βασιλόπιτα, _Vasilópita_, lit. '(St.) Basil-pie' or 'Vassilis pie', see below) is a [New Year's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Day "New Year's Day") bread, cake or pie in Greece and throughout Southeastern Europe which contains a hidden coin or trinket which gives good luck to the receiver, like the Western European king cake. It is associated with [Saint Basil's day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Basil's_day "Saint Basil's day"), 1 January, in most of Greece, but in some regions, the traditions surrounding a cake or pita with a hidden coin are attached to Epiphany or to Christmas. It is made of a variety of dough, depending on regional and family tradition, including tsoureki. In some families, instead of dough, it is made from a custard base called galatopita (literally milk-pita). In the Thessaly region a pork filled phyllo pie is made with a hidden coin. The pie is also known as _Chronópita_ (Χρονόπιτα < χρόνος: _chrónos ⇨ time/year_ + πίτα: _píta ⇨ pie_), meaning "New Year's pie".
In other areas of the Balkans, the tradition of cake with a hidden coin during winter holidays exists, but is not associated with Saint Basil at all. The practice is documented among Ukrainians (a pirog is cut); Romanians; Serbs ("česnica", eaten on Christmas); Albanians ("pite" or “kulaç”, eaten by both Christians and Muslims); Bulgarians (_pogacha_, _Novogodishna banitsa_ (for New Year's), _Svety Vasileva pogacha_); etc.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-hasluck-1)
texts.1:
On New Year's Day families cut the vasilopita to bless the house and bring good luck for the new year. This is usually done at the midnight of New Year's Eve. A coin is hidden in the bread by slipping it into the dough before baking. At midnight the sign of the cross is etched with a knife across the cake. A piece of cake is sliced for each member of the family and any visitors present at the time, by order of age from eldest to youngest. Slices are also cut for various symbolic people or groups, depending on local and family tradition. They may include the Lord, St. Basil and other saints, the poor, the household, or the Kallikantzaroi. In older times, the coin often was a valuable one, such as a gold sovereign. Nowadays there is often a prearranged gift, money, or otherwise, to be given to the coin recipient._[citation needed_]
Many private or public institutions, such as societies, clubs, workplaces, companies, etc., cut their vasilopita at a convenient time between New Year's Day and the beginning of the Great Fast, in celebrations that range from impromptu potluck gatherings to formal receptions or balls._[citation needed_]
Saint Basil's Feast Day is observed on 1 January, the beginning of the New Year and the Epiphany season known as the _Vasilopita Observance_._[citation needed_]
Margaret Hasluck (1927) disputes the historicity of the Greek folk tradition of celebrating the feast day of St. Basil with _vasilopita_. She says the popular belief is based on a "false etymology". Hasluck arrives at this conclusion by comparing the traditions of Greek-speaking communities with the western European celebrations of the Twelfth Night and Epiphany. Hasluck notes that no document mentions the _basilopita_, although Gregory of Nyssa confirms the festival of Basil was one of the feast days that succeeded Christmas in his time:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-hasluck-1)
> After [Christmas] the spiritual dance was opened by apostles and prophets...These are Stephen, Peter, James, John, and Paul. Then after them, in his due order, the pastor and teacher initiates our present gathering. Who is this? ... I mean Basil, the man of noble life and speech.
texts.2: Hasluck speculates that the etymology connecting the tradition to Basil's feast day is erroneous. She proposes that the translation "cake of the king" (from _basileus_) is as accurate as the translation "cake of basil", a claim that she says is supported by the similarity in customs of the hidden coin and the hidden bean. She refers to _Larousse Gastronomique'_ s description of the _fève_ custom referring to the _gateau des rois_ (popularly known as king cake in English) associated in present times with the Christian holiday of Epiphany celebrated on the "Twelfth Night" after Christmas. She disputes the Christian origin of the holiday: "We may safely dismiss the theory of their Christian origin and recognize, with many good authorities, in the Twelve Days the relics of a purely pagan festival." According to Hasluck, the pagan holiday of the Twelve Days is the same as the Roman Saturnalia: "One feature of the Saturnalia was that men drew for a king with a bean, and held high revelry under his leadership for the duration of the festivities", which she says is the same as the Greek festival Kronia: "Consequently, with some confidence we identify the Basil of the _basilopita_ with the _basileus_, the "king" of Saaturnalia".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-hasluck-1)
texts.3:
Nonetheless, in popular tradition, vasilopita is associated with a legend of Basil of Caesarea. According to one story, Basil called on the Roman citizens of Caesarea to raise a ransom payment to stop the siege of the city. Each member of the city gave whatever they had in gold and jewelry. When the ransom was raised, the enemy was so embarrassed by the act of collective giving that he called off the siege without collecting payment. Basil was then tasked with returning the unpaid ransom, but had no way to know which items belonged to which family so he baked all of the jewellery into loaves of bread and distributed the loaves to the city, and by a miracle each citizen received their exact share. In some tellings, the sieging tribal chief is replaced with an evil emperor levying a tax or simply with Basil attempting to give charity to the poor without embarrassing them.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-vasilopita.com-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-antiochian-3)_[better source needed_]
The name "βασιλόπιτα" comes from βασιλεύς 'king' + πίτα 'cake', but was reinterpreted as "Basil's (Βασίλειος) cake".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-hasluck-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-CFVM-5) In Cyprus it is also known as vasilopoulla ("βασιλοπούλλα").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-CFVM-5)

## The meaning of the vasilopita
Ever wonder why, in most Greek families, names seem to be on repeat? At any family function you are likely to find 4 Marias, 3 Costas and about 7 Georges. That’s because Greek parents have traditionally always named their children after their own parents. So, two siblings who each have daughters, may very well name their girls after their common mother, for example. Many Greek names are also names of Saints, making the Nameday (the day on which we commemorate the life of a given Saint) a much bigger deal amongst many Greeks than birthdays could ever be. Each of us is named after one of our grandmothers, and one of our Greek names (Vasiliki) is also associated with Saint Basil the Great, who is commemorated on January 1st, the day of his death.
St. Basil the Great was the Greek bishop of Caesarea Mazaca in Coppadocia, in Asia Minor (what is today, Turkey). In addition to his theological works, he was also a great support for the underprivileged and poor. In his memory, on St. Basil’s Day, homes of Orthodox Christians serve vasilopita (translated to mean _St. Basil’s bread_) to honour him. Although there are many versions and types of vasilopita, they all have one thing in common; there is a single coin baked into each one. This coin is a symbol and reminder of St. Basil’s intervention against the emperor of Caesarea, and God’s miracle. One year, the emperor of Caesarea had levied a heavy tax on the people, during a year of great famine and hardship. Upon hearing the news, St. Basil asked the emperor to repent, and he did. The emperor ordered that all gold coins, money and jewels that the people had used to pay this tax, be returned to them. Bishop Basil was assigned the daunting and overwhelming task of doing so. Unsure of how to return the goods to their rightful owners, prayer led St. Basil to bake a large pita, into which he inserted all the valuables. He then called the townspeople to each take a piece. Miraculously, each person received a piece of vasilopita that contained the exact items which were to be returned to them.

## How to serve vasilopita
In my family, vasilopita is always served after lunch on the Feast Day of St. Basil, which is coincidentally also New Year’s Day (January 1st) for many. Our father is typically the person who cuts and serves the pieces, and this is done in a particular order. The first piece is cut and saved for Christ, the second for St. Basil, and the third for the less fortunate. Then, a piece of vasilopita is cut for all members of the family, and any friends who may be present. The vasilopita is always offered first to the oldest person present, up until the youngest. The person whose piece contains the coin is expected to have good luck and blessings for the upcoming year.

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Mix your batter carefully
Unlike cooking, where you can take some liberties, and perhaps even some shortcuts, baking really is a science. There are many pitfalls you can encounter when baking, which is why it is important to find reliable recipes (like the ones here at Mia Kouppa) and follow them carefully.
One of the important things to keep in mind when you are making vasilopita is how the batter comes together. Sometimes you will bake a cake and end up with streaks, or areas of dense, sodden cake. These give the impression that the cake is under-baked – even though it’s completely baked. In order to prevent this from happening, you must beat together the sugar, butter and eggs, slowly; your mixer should not go any higher than medium speed.
Then, when you add the dry ingredients, the mixing speed has to be slower still. By keeping the mixer speed at medium and lower you avoid developing the flour’s gluten too much; which will help avoid your cake sinking in the middle once you take it out of the oven. It is this sinking which creates dense, moist, gluey streaks in your cake. .

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### How to prepare your cake pan
Although you will grease your cake pan with some vegetable oil, is it still a very good idea to line the bottom of the pan with parchment paper. The easiest way to get just the right size of parchment paper for the bottom of your round pan is to place your baking pan on a sheet of parchment paper and to trace its outline with a pencil. Then, use a scissor to cut out the perfect circle. Ta da!

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Inserting the coin into your cake batter
Before inserting the coin into your cake batter, it is a very good idea to wash it and to then wrap it with either food grade plastic wrap or aluminum foil. You can even use parchment paper, although that can be a little more cumbersome to wrap the coin in. Traditionally, before inserting the coin into the cake you would use it to make the sign of the cross over the pan. The easiest way to get your coin into the batter is to use a knife to make a small cut into the batter and slip the coin right in. Spread the batter evenly so that it is not obvious where the coin is.

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### How to display the year on your vasilopita
There are many ways to bake a vasilopita. Some versions are very bread-like, and similar to the Easter tsoureki. Other versions, like this recipe, are more cake-like. Both are delicious, but different. Besides the obvious flavour and texture differences, another difference between the two is that with the bread type of vasilopita you can usually use a bit of the dough to roll out the numbers of the year, which is then laid on top of the bread before baking. You can’t really do that with this recipe. If you would like to have the year showcased on your vasilopita however, you can either decorate it with sliced almonds, or use a stencil with the year cut out of it, on top of the cake before you sprinkle it with icing sugar. My parents would sometimes do this, but not usually. They always reminded us that this was not a New Year’s cake, but a cake to commemorate the Feast Day of St. Basil.

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Serve and eat your vasilopita with care
Eating cake or bread with a coin hidden in it could definitely be a choking hazard, so please…if you are serving vasilopita to the very young or the very elderly, be careful. I remember that when me and my siblings were little, our parents would often tear our pieces apart before allowing us to eat them, being sure that if there was a coin in our piece, it would be found before it ended up in our mouths. Now that I think of it…I can’t remember a year when one of the children didn’t actually get the coin. Coincidence? Maybe…or perhaps clever serving by our dad. It was always such a thrill to find the coin!

## Baking tips and helpful hints
### Best when served the day after it is made
This cake keeps really well and is even more delicious if made the day before. This is also a great option because it means that your cake will have ample time to cool fully before you sprinkle it with icing sugar.

## Recipe variations
### Make vasilopita cupcakes
If you will only be a few people gathering in New Year’s Day it is hard to divide up the vasilopita completely in order to be sure that someone gets the coin. There ends up being a lot of wasted cake if, for example, four people share the entire vasilopita.
That is why there are vasilopita cupcakes! Learn how to make this not-quite-traditional-but-absolutely-brilliant version of vasilopita. This way you ensure that the coin will be found, everyone has an appropriate amount of the vasilopita, and there is no waste! Learn how to make them by following this recipe for vasilopita cupcakes.

**Vasilopita** (Greek: Βασιλόπιτα, _Vasilópita_, lit. '(St.) Basil-pie' or 'Vassilis pie', see below) is a [New Year's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Day "New Year's Day") bread, cake or pie in Greece and throughout Southeastern Europe which contains a hidden coin or trinket which gives good luck to the receiver, like the Western European king cake. It is associated with [Saint Basil's day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Basil's_day "Saint Basil's day"), 1 January, in most of Greece, but in some regions, the traditions surrounding a cake or pita with a hidden coin are attached to Epiphany or to Christmas. It is made of a variety of dough, depending on regional and family tradition, including tsoureki. In some families, instead of dough, it is made from a custard base called galatopita (literally milk-pita). In the Thessaly region a pork filled phyllo pie is made with a hidden coin. The pie is also known as _Chronópita_ (Χρονόπιτα < χρόνος: _chrónos ⇨ time/year_ + πίτα: _píta ⇨ pie_), meaning "New Year's pie".
In other areas of the Balkans, the tradition of cake with a hidden coin during winter holidays exists, but is not associated with Saint Basil at all. The practice is documented among Ukrainians (a pirog is cut); Romanians; Serbs ("česnica", eaten on Christmas); Albanians ("pite" or “kulaç”, eaten by both Christians and Muslims); Bulgarians (_pogacha_, _Novogodishna banitsa_ (for New Year's), _Svety Vasileva pogacha_); etc.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-hasluck-1)

On New Year's Day families cut the vasilopita to bless the house and bring good luck for the new year. This is usually done at the midnight of New Year's Eve. A coin is hidden in the bread by slipping it into the dough before baking. At midnight the sign of the cross is etched with a knife across the cake. A piece of cake is sliced for each member of the family and any visitors present at the time, by order of age from eldest to youngest. Slices are also cut for various symbolic people or groups, depending on local and family tradition. They may include the Lord, St. Basil and other saints, the poor, the household, or the Kallikantzaroi. In older times, the coin often was a valuable one, such as a gold sovereign. Nowadays there is often a prearranged gift, money, or otherwise, to be given to the coin recipient._[citation needed_]
Many private or public institutions, such as societies, clubs, workplaces, companies, etc., cut their vasilopita at a convenient time between New Year's Day and the beginning of the Great Fast, in celebrations that range from impromptu potluck gatherings to formal receptions or balls._[citation needed_]
Saint Basil's Feast Day is observed on 1 January, the beginning of the New Year and the Epiphany season known as the _Vasilopita Observance_._[citation needed_]
Margaret Hasluck (1927) disputes the historicity of the Greek folk tradition of celebrating the feast day of St. Basil with _vasilopita_. She says the popular belief is based on a "false etymology". Hasluck arrives at this conclusion by comparing the traditions of Greek-speaking communities with the western European celebrations of the Twelfth Night and Epiphany. Hasluck notes that no document mentions the _basilopita_, although Gregory of Nyssa confirms the festival of Basil was one of the feast days that succeeded Christmas in his time:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-hasluck-1)
> After [Christmas] the spiritual dance was opened by apostles and prophets...These are Stephen, Peter, James, John, and Paul. Then after them, in his due order, the pastor and teacher initiates our present gathering. Who is this? ... I mean Basil, the man of noble life and speech.

Hasluck speculates that the etymology connecting the tradition to Basil's feast day is erroneous. She proposes that the translation "cake of the king" (from _basileus_) is as accurate as the translation "cake of basil", a claim that she says is supported by the similarity in customs of the hidden coin and the hidden bean. She refers to _Larousse Gastronomique'_ s description of the _fève_ custom referring to the _gateau des rois_ (popularly known as king cake in English) associated in present times with the Christian holiday of Epiphany celebrated on the "Twelfth Night" after Christmas. She disputes the Christian origin of the holiday: "We may safely dismiss the theory of their Christian origin and recognize, with many good authorities, in the Twelve Days the relics of a purely pagan festival." According to Hasluck, the pagan holiday of the Twelve Days is the same as the Roman Saturnalia: "One feature of the Saturnalia was that men drew for a king with a bean, and held high revelry under his leadership for the duration of the festivities", which she says is the same as the Greek festival Kronia: "Consequently, with some confidence we identify the Basil of the _basilopita_ with the _basileus_, the "king" of Saaturnalia".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilopita#cite_note-hasluck-1)

Nonetheless, in popular tradition, vasilopita is associated with a legend of Basil of Caesarea. According to one story, Basil called on the Roman citizens of Caesarea to raise a ransom payment to stop the siege of the city. Each member of the city gave whatever they had in gold and jewelry. When the ransom was raised, the enemy was so embarrassed by the act of collective giving that he called off the siege without collecting payment. Basil was then tasked with returning the unpaid ransom, but had no way to know which items belonged to which family so he baked all of the jewellery into loaves of bread and distributed the loaves to the city, and by a miracle each citizen received their exact share. ## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
Constantine funded two churches. Helena identified two sites. What grew out of that beginning, across the following three centuries, was something on an entirely different scale: city walls paid for by an empress in exile, one of the largest basilicas in the Christian world raised on Justinian's orders, a Judean desert filling with hermits and monasteries, and pilgrims arriving from Gaul and Spain and Egypt in numbers large enough to require purpose-built hospices along the road.
Our companion article on **Constantine, Helena, and the transformation of Christianity** covers the founding moment; this article covers everything that followed — the period historians call Byzantine, running from the early fourth century until the region passed out of Christian imperial control in the seventh century.
It is the era that gave Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Galilee, and the Judean Desert much of the sacred architecture, monastic culture, and pilgrimage geography that still shape how Christians experience the **Holy Land**today. Some of its greatest buildings disappeared. Others were rebuilt repeatedly. A few institutions survived in astonishing continuity. Together they created a Christian landscape whose outlines remained visible long after Byzantine political rule itself had vanished.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### What "Byzantine" Means for the Holy Land
"Byzantine" is a modern historians' label, not a term the people of the period used for themselves; they called their empire Roman, and it remained the eastern continuation of the Roman Empire long after imperial government disappeared in the West. For the Holy Land, the Byzantine period runs conventionally from Constantine's reign through the region's loss to the Muslim conquest in the seventh century — roughly three hundred years during which an empire that had once periodically persecuted Christians increasingly identified itself with Christianity.
A major step came in 380 under Emperor Theodosius I, when the Edict of Thessalonica gave imperial endorsement to the Nicene form of Christianity. It went significantly beyond Constantine's earlier policy of toleration, although the establishment of Nicene Christianity as the dominant imperial orthodoxy was a process rather than something completed by a single decree. The theological background reached back to the **Council of Nicaea in 325**, whose confession concerning Christ became a defining reference point in the doctrinal struggles of the fourth century.
What followed was not a single sustained building boom but successive waves of imperial and private patronage, monastic expansion, pilgrimage development, and local Christian institution-building, punctuated by real crises — plague, religious conflict, revolt, and eventually invasion — that this article does not smooth over. The Holy Land was becoming more visibly Christian, but that transformation took place within a religiously diverse population and was neither peaceful nor uncontested at every stage.
The Christian landscape of the Byzantine period was the result of a much longer story that had begun centuries earlier in Jerusalem. Our guide to **how Christianity began in Jerusalem and developed into the early Church** traces that foundation, before imperial patronage, monumental churches, and organized pilgrimage transformed the Holy Land so dramatically.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Empress Eudocia and the Walls of a Christian City
Aelia Eudocia, wife of the eastern emperor Theodosius II, first visited Jerusalem on pilgrimage in 438 and returned permanently around 443, after a falling-out with her husband's court that historians still debate the exact cause of. Whatever drove her there, she spent the final years of her life, until her death in 460, as one of Jerusalem's most significant patrons. She funded major building and charitable projects associated with the city's expanding Christian life, including new fortifications, a basilica honoring Saint Stephen, the Church's first martyr, and institutions serving the poor and the growing stream of pilgrims.
Eudocia's Jerusalem matters for a reason beyond any single building: she represents a shift from the emperor's-mother pilgrimage that Helena had modeled a century earlier toward something more permanent — an imperial figure who did not simply visit and depart, but relocated her life to the city and spent years embedding Christian institutions into its physical fabric.
The result belonged to a much broader change in **Jerusalem's development as Christianity's sacred city**. The Jerusalem encountered by fourth-century pilgrims had already been transformed by Constantine's churches. By Eudocia's lifetime, pilgrimage, charitable institutions, monastic communities, relic cults, liturgical processions, and imperial patronage were turning the city into something more elaborate: not simply a place containing Christian holy sites, but an urban landscape increasingly organized around Christian sacred memory.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Justinian's Jerusalem: The Nea Church and an Empire's Ambition
A century after Eudocia, Emperor Justinian brought a different kind of ambition to Jerusalem — the same instinct for monumental building he applied to Constantinople's Hagia Sophia. His Nea Church, formally the Church of the Theotokos, was consecrated in Jerusalem on November 20, 543, and by the account of Procopius, Justinian's own court historian, its construction required specially built roads and forty-ox teams to haul stone blocks and cedar timbers of extraordinary size from as far as Lebanon. It ranked among the largest church buildings anywhere in the Christian world at the time.
The Nea did not survive the centuries that followed, but twentieth-century excavations uncovered substantial remains, including massive foundation walls and a Greek dedicatory inscription explicitly naming Justinian. The discovery was unusually important because it allowed archaeology, literary description, and the surviving Byzantine representation of Jerusalem to illuminate one another.
Justinian's building program extended well beyond Jerusalem. He also rebuilt the **Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem** during the sixth century, replacing the earlier Constantinian basilica with the structure that forms the essential core of the church standing there today. The result is one of the most remarkable survivals of Byzantine Christian architecture anywhere in the Holy Land.
One further monument from this period deserves mention for what it tells historians rather than what it once looked like: the sixth-century mosaic floor map discovered in a church at Madaba, in modern Jordan. The **Madaba Map** depicts a wide sweep of the biblical lands, but its image of Jerusalem is especially detailed. The city appears from a kind of elevated perspective, with gates, streets, churches, and major monuments arranged so that a viewer standing over the mosaic could recognize the sacred geography of Byzantine Jerusalem.
Its representation of the city is not simply decorative. The great colonnaded street can be followed through the urban center; the Holy Sepulchre is prominently represented; and the Nea Church appears within the southern part of the city. For archaeologists, this sixth-century mosaic became something remarkably close to an ancient visual guide. When modern excavations uncovered the Nea's remains, the location shown on the Madaba Map helped make sense of the buried Byzantine city.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Justinian's Jerusalem: The Nea Church and an Empire's Ambition
The map also reveals how dramatically Christian priorities had reshaped Jerusalem's visual identity. A Roman city that had once been rebuilt as Aelia Capitolina was now being represented through its churches and Christian sacred places. The **Church of the Holy Sepulchre** occupies a conspicuous place in that image, reflecting the importance the Constantinian sanctuary had acquired at the heart of Christian Jerusalem. The Madaba mosaic is therefore more than an old map: it is a surviving picture of how Byzantine Christians imagined the Holy City itself.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Beyond Jerusalem: Bethlehem, Galilee, and a Christianized Landscape
Some sites preserve especially complicated layers of history. Magdala, Mount Tabor, Arbel, and Kursi each tell somewhat different stories about Jewish settlement, Christian pilgrimage, monastic life, and the later identification of biblical places. Our guide to **Magdala, Mount Tabor, Arbel, and Kursi** explores those sites individually. Seen together, however, they reveal the larger Byzantine pattern: the Christianization of the Holy Land was not the construction of one sacred capital in Jerusalem, but the gradual creation of an interconnected landscape extending from Judea through Bethlehem and north into Galilee.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Cracks in the Byzantine Peace: Revolt and the Persian Invasion
This was not, across three centuries, an uninterrupted story of peaceful construction. The Samaritan community of central Palestine, resentful of policies that increasingly restricted its position under a Christian empire, rose in a series of major revolts in the fifth and sixth centuries, including a particularly serious uprising in 529. The revolts were suppressed with considerable violence and contributed to a long-term decline in the Samaritan population. They are an important reminder that Byzantine Palestine's increasingly Christian public identity existed alongside Jewish, Samaritan, and other communities and could be imposed and contested rather than universally embraced.
The more decisive crisis came from outside the empire. In 614, Sasanian Persian forces captured Jerusalem during the great Byzantine-Sasanian war. Christian sources describe severe destruction and loss of life, although the precise scale and details remain subjects of historical and archaeological debate. Major Christian buildings were damaged, and the relic venerated in Jerusalem as the **True Cross** was carried away by the Persians.
Emperor Heraclius eventually reversed the war dramatically, forcing the Sasanian Empire into peace and recovering the relic. Its ceremonial restoration to Jerusalem at the end of the 620s or beginning of the 630s became one of the great symbolic moments of late Byzantine Christian memory. The episode further strengthened the association between Jerusalem, imperial power, and the Cross — an association whose much earlier origins are explored in our article on **Constantine and Saint Helena**.
The **Church of the Holy Sepulchre**, damaged during the Persian conquest, was repaired under the leadership traditionally associated with Modestus of Jerusalem. It would not be the last reconstruction. Fire, invasion, deliberate destruction, earthquakes, political changes, and competing Christian custodians would repeatedly alter the complex across the centuries, making the church standing today a physical record of Jerusalem's turbulent Christian history rather than a perfectly preserved fourth-century monument.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### The End of Byzantine Jerusalem
Byzantine control had barely been restored after the Persian war when armies emerging from Arabia transformed the political map of the Near East. Byzantine forces suffered a decisive defeat at the Battle of Yarmouk in 636, after which Muslim armies consolidated control over much of Syria and Palestine. Jerusalem eventually negotiated terms of surrender, probably in **638**, although 637 also appears in traditional chronologies. Patriarch Sophronius was still leading Jerusalem's Christian community as Byzantine political authority in the city came to an end.
Later Christian and Muslim traditions connect Caliph Umar personally with Jerusalem's surrender and with guarantees protecting Christian lives, property, and places of worship. The exact wording and development of the various agreements associated with Umar are historically complex, and later documents should not simply be treated as verbatim transcripts of a single seventh-century treaty. What is clear is that Jerusalem passed into Muslim rule without experiencing the kind of destruction associated with the Persian capture of 614, and Christian institutions continued functioning under the new political order.
One famous later tradition tells that Patriarch Sophronius invited Umar to pray inside the **Church of the Holy Sepulchre** and that the caliph declined, fearing that later Muslims might use his prayer there as grounds to convert the church into a mosque. The story became an enduring part of Jerusalem's memory and appears in later historical accounts, but it should be understood as a tradition transmitted after the conquest rather than a securely documented eyewitness episode from 638. Medieval Muslim memory nevertheless associated Umar with the protection of Christian holy places in Jerusalem.
What changed decisively was political control, not the immediate disappearance of Christian Jerusalem. Churches continued to function. Pilgrims continued to arrive. Monasteries such as Mar Saba remained active. Local Christians had to learn how to live within a new Islamic political order, but the Christian sacred geography created during the Byzantine centuries survived the empire that had built so much of it. Scholarship on Palestine's transition from Byzantine to Islamic rule increasingly emphasizes this combination of political rupture and substantial local continuity.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### What the Byzantine Holy Land Left Behind
The Byzantine centuries did not simply disappear when imperial rule ended; they left behind the physical and institutional skeleton that later Christian history in the Holy Land would keep building upon. The Church of the Nativity standing in Bethlehem today preserves the essential form of Justinian's sixth-century basilica. Mar Saba remains an active monastery rooted in the community Sabas founded some fifteen centuries ago. The Madaba Map still gives archaeologists an extraordinary image of the region's Christian topography. And beneath modern Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee, Byzantine walls, mosaics, foundations, cisterns, tombs, and inscriptions continue to emerge.
The period also helped shape forms of Eastern Christian life that survived the loss of Byzantine political control. Greek-speaking ecclesiastical traditions, monastic liturgy, the veneration of sacred places, and long-established Christian communities remained part of the region under successive rulers. That continuity forms an important part of the later history explored in our guide to the **Eastern Orthodox Church** and its relationship with the Holy Land.
Sacred images were part of that inheritance, and the long quarrel over whether Christians could make and venerate them is told in our guide to **the meaning of Byzantine and Christian icons**.
Perhaps the most enduring Byzantine legacy, however, is less obvious than any individual building. These centuries helped establish the basic Christian map of the Holy Land. Jerusalem meant the Holy Sepulchre, the Mount of Olives, Gethsemane, and a sequence of places through which Christ's Passion could be remembered. Bethlehem centered Christian memory on the Nativity. Galilee became a landscape through which Gospel episodes could be followed from site to site. The Judean Desert became inseparable from monastic Christianity. Pilgrimage joined these places together.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### What the Byzantine Holy Land Left Behind
The centuries after the Muslim conquest brought new rulers, new cultural worlds, periods of coexistence and conflict, and eventually the arrival of Latin Christian armies that captured Jerusalem in 1099. The **Crusades and the Holy Land** belong to a very different political and religious age. Yet the Jerusalem those armies fought over, and the Bethlehem and Galilee that later pilgrims sought, still rested heavily upon the sacred geography formed during the Byzantine centuries — by emperors and empresses, bishops and monks, craftsmen and donors, travelers like Egeria, and countless Christians whose names have disappeared while the places they helped shape remain.

### Frequently Asked Questions
#### What is meant by the "Byzantine Holy Land"?
It refers to the roughly three centuries, from the early fourth century to the Muslim conquest in the seventh century, when the Holy Land formed part of the Christian Roman Empire and Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Galilee, and the Judean Desert were extensively developed with churches, monasteries, and pilgrim infrastructure.

### Frequently Asked Questions
#### Who was Empress Eudocia and what did she build in Jerusalem?
Eudocia was a fifth-century Roman empress who eventually settled in Jerusalem. She became one of the city's major Christian patrons, associated with new fortifications, churches including a basilica honoring Saint Stephen, and charitable institutions serving the poor and pilgrims.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Frequently Asked Questions
#### What was Justinian's Nea Church?
The Nea Church, consecrated in Jerusalem in 543, was an enormous basilica funded by Emperor Justinian. Procopius described its construction as a major engineering undertaking, and substantial remains of the church were uncovered by twentieth-century archaeologists.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Frequently Asked Questions
#### Why did so many monks settle in the Judean Desert?
Beginning in the fourth century, ascetics such as Chariton, Euthymius, and later Sabas were drawn to the desert's isolation as a place for prayer and solitude close to Jerusalem's holy sites. Their communities developed into an extensive monastic landscape that included Mar Saba.

### Frequently Asked Questions
#### What happened to Jerusalem during the Persian invasion of 614?
Sasanian Persian forces captured Jerusalem in 614, and many Christian buildings were damaged or destroyed. The relic venerated as the True Cross was carried away. Byzantine forces later recovered the relic, which was ceremonially restored to Jerusalem during the reign of Emperor Heraclius.

### Frequently Asked Questions
#### What happened to Jerusalem's Christians after the Muslim conquest?
Jerusalem negotiated terms of surrender during the Muslim conquest, probably in 638. Christian communities, churches, monasteries, and pilgrimage continued under Muslim rule, although the political framework of the Holy Land had fundamentally changed.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Closing Reflection
What strikes anyone who spends time with this period is how much of it survives by accident as much as design. An empress's exile becomes a chapter in Jerusalem's walls. A court historian's boast about ox-teams becomes a rare written witness to a church otherwise reduced to foundation stones. A traveler's reports to distant Christian women become the clearest window historians have into how Jerusalem prayed sixteen centuries ago. A mosaic floor in Jordan preserves a map of a city whose Byzantine streets and monuments would otherwise be far harder to reconstruct.
And then there is Mar Saba. Monks still descend the same desert gorge where Sabas established his community in the fifth century, long after the emperors who ruled the Holy Land disappeared. Bethlehem's great basilica still rises above the traditional place of Christ's birth. Christians still gather at the Holy Sepulchre. Pilgrims still move between Jerusalem, Bethlehem, the Mount of Olives, and Galilee, following a sacred geography that Byzantine Christians helped give physical form.
Empires rise in this story and empires fall — Roman rule becomes Christian Roman rule, Jerusalem falls to Persia and returns to Byzantium, and Byzantine authority finally gives way to Muslim government. Yet the churches, desert cells, pilgrim roads, mosaics, liturgies, and memories outlasted the political world that created them.
That may be the Byzantine Holy Land's most enduring legacy. It did not create Christianity's attachment to Jerusalem, Bethlehem, or Galilee. Those memories reached back to the beginnings of the faith. What the Byzantine centuries did was give those memories architecture, roads, monasteries, processions, mosaics, institutions, and a landscape through which Christians could physically walk.
Much of that landscape is still there.

## Byzantium
The term “Byzantine” derives from Byzantium, an ancient Greek colony founded by a man named Byzas. Located on the European side of the Bosporus (the strait linking the Black Sea to the Mediterranean), the site of Byzantium was ideally located to serve as a transit and trade point between Europe and Asia.
In A.D. 330, Roman Emperor Constantine I chose Byzantium as the site of a “New Rome” with an eponymous capital city, Constantinople. Five years earlier, at the Council of Nicaea, Constantine had established Christianity — once an obscure Jewish sect — as Rome’s official religion.
The citizens of Constantinople and the rest of the Eastern Roman Empire identified strongly as Romans and Christians, though many of them spoke Greek and not Latin.

## Did you know?
One of the most extraordinary aspects of the Byzantine Empire was its longevity: It was the only organized state west of China to survive without interruption from ancient times until the beginning of the modern age.
Though Constantine ruled over a unified Roman Empire, this unity proved illusory after his death in 337. In 364, Emperor Valentinian I again divided the empire into western and eastern sections, putting himself in power in the west and his brother Valens in the east.
The fate of the two regions diverged greatly over the next several centuries. In the west, constant attacks from German invaders such as the Visigoths broke the struggling empire down piece by piece until Italy was the only territory left under Roman control. In 476, the barbarian Odoacer overthrew the last Roman emperor, Romulus Augustus, and after many centuries, the once-mighty empire of Rome had fallen.

## Byzantine Empire Flourishes
With Constantinople located on a strait, it was extremely difficult to breach the capital’s defenses; in addition, the eastern empire had a much smaller common frontier with Europe.
It also benefited greatly from a stronger administrative center and internal political stability, as well as great wealth compared with other states of the early medieval period. The eastern emperors were able to exert more control over the empire’s economic resources and more effectively muster sufficient manpower to combat invasion.

## Eastern Roman Empire
As a result of these advantages, the Eastern Roman Empire, variously known as the Byzantine Empire or Byzantium, was able to survive for centuries after the fall of Rome.
Though Byzantium was ruled by Roman law and Roman political institutions, and its official language was Latin, Greek was also widely spoken, and students received education in Greek history, literature and culture.

## Council of Chalcedon
In terms of religion, the Council of Chalcedon in 451 officially established the division of the Christian world into separate patriarchates, including Rome (where the patriarch would later call himself pope), Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem.
Even after the Islamic empire absorbed Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem in the seventh century, the Byzantine emperor would remain the spiritual leader of most eastern Christians.

## Justinian I
Justinian I, who took power in 527 and would rule until his death in 565, was the first great ruler of the Byzantine Empire. During the years of his reign, the empire included most of the land surrounding the Mediterranean Sea, as Justinian’s armies conquered part of the former Western Roman Empire, including North Africa.
At the time of Justinian’s death, the Byzantine Empire reigned supreme as the largest and most powerful state in Europe. Debts incurred through war had left the empire in dire financial straits, however, and his successors were forced to heavily tax Byzantine citizens in order to keep the empire afloat.
In addition, the imperial army was stretched too thin, and would struggle in vain to maintain the territory conquered during Justinian’s rule. During the seventh and eighth centuries, attacks from the Persian Empire and from Slavs, combined with internal political instability and economic regression, threatened the vast empire.
A new, even more serious threat arose in the form of Islam, founded by the prophet Muhammad in Mecca in 622. In 634, Muslim armies began their assault on the Byzantine Empire by storming into Syria.
By the end of the century, Byzantium would lose Syria, the Holy Land, Egypt and North Africa (among other territories) to Islamic forces.

## Iconoclasm
During the eighth and early ninth centuries, Byzantine emperors (beginning with Leo III in 730) spearheaded a movement that denied the holiness of icons, or religious images, and prohibited their worship or veneration.
Known as Iconoclasm—literally “the smashing of images”—the movement waxed and waned under various rulers, but did not end definitively until 843, when a Church council under Emperor Michael III ruled in favor of the display of religious images.

## Byzantine Art
During the late 10th and early 11th centuries, under the rule of the Macedonian dynasty founded by Michael III’s successor, Basil, the Byzantine Empire enjoyed a golden age.
Though it stretched over less territory, Byzantium had more control over trade, more wealth and more international prestige than under Justinian. The strong imperial government patronized Byzantine art, including now-cherished Byzantine mosaics.
Greek became the official language of the state, and a flourishing culture of monasticism was centered on Mount Athos in northeastern Greece. Monks administered many institutions (orphanages, schools, hospitals) in everyday life, and Byzantine missionaries won many converts to Christianity among the Slavic peoples of the central and eastern Balkans (including Bulgaria and Serbia) and Russia.

## The Crusades
The end of the 11th century saw the beginning of the Crusades, the series of holy wars waged by European Christians against Muslims in the Near East from 1095 to 1291.
With the Seijuk Turks of central Asia bearing down on Constantinople, Emperor Alexius I turned to the West for help, resulting in the declaration of “holy war” by Pope Urban II at Clermont, France, that began the First Crusade.
As armies from France, Germany and Italy poured into Byzantium, Alexius tried to force their leaders to swear an oath of loyalty to him in order to guarantee that land regained from the Turks would be restored to his empire. After Western and Byzantine forces recaptured Nicaea in Asia Minor from the Turks, Alexius and his army retreated, drawing accusations of betrayal from the Crusaders.
During the subsequent Crusades, animosity continued to build between Byzantium and the West, culminating in the conquest and looting of Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade in 1204.
The Latin regime established in Constantinople existed on shaky ground due to the open hostility of the city’s population and its lack of money. Many refugees from Constantinople fled to Nicaea, site of a Byzantine government-in-exile that would retake the capital and overthrow Latin rule in 1261.

## Fall of Constantinople
During the rule of the Palaiologan emperors, beginning with Michael VIII in 1261, the economy of the once-mighty Byzantine state was crippled, and never regained its former stature.
As a vassal state, Byzantium paid tribute to the sultan and provided him with military support. Under John’s successors, the empire gained sporadic relief from Ottoman oppression, but the rise of Murad II as sultan in 1421 marked the end of the final respite.
Murad revoked all privileges given to the Byzantines and laid siege to Constantinople; his successor, Mehmed II, completed this process when he launched the final attack on the city. On May 29, 1453, after an Ottoman army stormed Constantinople, Mehmed triumphantly entered the Hagia Sophia, which would soon be converted to the city’s leading mosque.
The fall of Constantinople marked the end of a glorious era for the Byzantine Empire. Emperor Constantine XI died in battle that day, and the Byzantine Empire collapsed, ushering in the long reign of the Ottoman Empire.

## Legacy of the Byzantine Empire
In the centuries leading up to the final Ottoman conquest in 1453, the culture of the Byzantine Empire–including literature, art, architecture, law and theology–flourished even as the empire itself faltered.
Byzantine culture would exert a great influence on the Western intellectual tradition, as scholars of the Renaissance sought help from Byzantine scholars in translating Greek pagan and Christian writings. (This process would continue after 1453, when many of these scholars fled from fallen Constantinople to Italy.)
Long after its end, Byzantine culture and civilization continued to exercise an influence on countries that practiced its Eastern Orthodox religion, including Russia, Romania, Bulgaria, Serbia and Greece, among others.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### What "Byzantine" Means for the Holy Land
"Byzantine" is a modern historians' label, not a term the people of the period used for themselves; they called their empire Roman, and it remained the eastern continuation of the Roman Empire long after imperial government disappeared in the West. For the Holy Land, the Byzantine period runs conventionally from Constantine's reign through the region's loss to the Muslim conquest in the seventh century — roughly three hundred years during which an empire that had once periodically persecuted Christians increasingly identified itself with Christianity.
A major step came in 380 under Emperor Theodosius I, when the Edict of Thessalonica gave imperial endorsement to the Nicene form of Christianity. It went significantly beyond Constantine's earlier policy of toleration, although the establishment of Nicene Christianity as the dominant imperial orthodoxy was a process rather than something completed by a single decree. The theological background reached back to the **Council of Nicaea in 325**, whose confession concerning Christ became a defining reference point in the doctrinal struggles of the fourth century.
What followed was not a single sustained building boom but successive waves of imperial and private patronage, monastic expansion, pilgrimage development, and local Christian institution-building, punctuated by real crises — plague, religious conflict, revolt, and eventually invasion — that this article does not smooth over. The Holy Land was becoming more visibly Christian, but that transformation took place within a religiously diverse population and was neither peaceful nor uncontested at every stage.
The Christian landscape of the Byzantine period was the result of a much longer story that had begun centuries earlier in Jerusalem. Our guide to **how Christianity began in Jerusalem and developed into the early Church** traces that foundation, before imperial patronage, monumental churches, and organized pilgrimage transformed the Holy Land so dramatically.
